questions.question_text: Which statement best defines nutrition?

choices.text: The study of food preparation and cooking methods only
The process by which the body obtains and uses nutrients for growth, maintenance and health
The administration of medicines to prevent diseases
The study of microorganisms found in food

questions.rationale: Nutrition involves the intake, digestion, absorption, metabolism and utilisation of nutrients by the body. These processes support energy production, growth, tissue repair and maintenance of normal body functions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered a balanced diet?

choices.text: A diet consisting mainly of carbohydrates
A diet containing adequate amounts of essential nutrients in appropriate proportions
A diet containing only fruits and vegetables
A diet that excludes all fats and proteins

questions.rationale: A balanced diet provides the energy and essential nutrients required by the body in appropriate amounts and proportions. Its composition should reflect an individual's age, physiological condition, activity level and health needs.

questions.question_text: Which macronutrient is the body's primary and preferred source of energy under normal conditions?
questions.rationale: Carbohydrates are broken down into simple sugars, including glucose, which cells use to produce energy. They provide approximately 4 kilocalories per gram.

questions.question_text: Which macronutrient is primarily required for growth and repair of body tissues?
questions.rationale: Proteins provide amino acids needed for the synthesis and repair of body tissues. They are also required for the production of enzymes, hormones and antibodies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following provides the highest amount of energy per gram?
questions.rationale: Fats provide approximately 9 kilocalories per gram, compared with about 4 kilocalories per gram from carbohydrates and proteins. They also support insulation, cell membrane structure and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.question_text: Which vitamin is essential for normal blood clotting?
questions.rationale: Vitamin K is necessary for the synthesis of several blood-clotting factors in the liver. Deficiency can impair coagulation and increase the risk of bleeding.

questions.question_text: Which mineral is an essential component of haemoglobin?
questions.rationale: Iron forms part of the haem group in haemoglobin, allowing red blood cells to transport oxygen. Inadequate iron intake or absorption can contribute to iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.question_text: Which vitamin is particularly important for calcium absorption and bone mineralisation?
questions.rationale: Vitamin D promotes intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, which are essential for bone mineralisation. Severe deficiency in children can cause rickets, while deficiency in adults can contribute to osteomalacia.

questions.question_text: Which measurement is commonly used to assess nutritional status in adults by relating body weight to height?
questions.rationale: Body mass index (BMI) is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. It is a screening measure used to classify adult weight status, although it does not directly measure body fat or nutritional deficiencies.

questions.question_text: Which clinical feature is classically associated with kwashiorkor?
questions.rationale: Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition characterised by bilateral pitting oedema. Other features may include skin changes, hair changes, poor appetite and growth failure.

questions.question_text: Which feature is most characteristic of marasmus?

choices.text: Generalised oedema as the defining feature
Severe wasting with marked loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat

questions.rationale: Marasmus is a form of severe acute malnutrition characterised by severe wasting and loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat. Unlike kwashiorkor, bilateral pitting oedema is not its defining feature.

questions.question_text: Which nutritional deficiency is the main cause of nutritional night blindness?
questions.rationale: Vitamin A is required for the formation of visual pigments involved in vision under low-light conditions. Deficiency can cause night blindness and, in severe cases, xerophthalmia and corneal damage.

questions.question_text: Which dietary modification is generally recommended for a patient with hypertension?

choices.text: Increased intake of highly salted foods
Reduced sodium intake and increased consumption of suitable fruits and vegetables

questions.rationale: Reducing dietary sodium can help lower blood pressure, while a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables and appropriate whole grains supports cardiovascular health. The DASH dietary approach is one recognised pattern for managing hypertension.

questions.question_text: Which dietary principle is important in the nutritional management of diabetes mellitus?

choices.text: Consuming large quantities of refined sugar at each meal
Consistent carbohydrate intake with appropriate portion control
Replacing all meals with fruit juice

questions.rationale: Consistent carbohydrate intake and appropriate portion control help manage post-meal blood glucose levels. Meal planning should also consider total energy needs, fibre intake, medication and physical activity.

questions.question_text: Which nutrient is particularly important before conception and during early pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects?
questions.rationale: Folic acid is essential for DNA synthesis and normal neural tube development in the early embryo. Women planning pregnancy are advised to take folic acid supplementation before conception and during early pregnancy according to national guidance.

questions.question_text: For how long should an infant be exclusively breastfed, according to WHO and standard infant-feeding recommendations?
questions.rationale: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life. At six months, safe and nutritionally adequate complementary foods should be introduced while breastfeeding continues.

questions.question_text: Which practice is most effective in reducing foodborne infection during food preparation?

choices.text: Using the same unwashed knife for raw meat and cooked food
Washing hands and preventing cross-contamination between raw and cooked foods
Storing raw meat above ready-to-eat foods

questions.rationale: Handwashing and separation of raw and cooked foods reduce the transfer of pathogenic microorganisms. Safe food storage, adequate cooking and clean utensils are also essential food safety practices.

questions.question_text: A student eats banku with okro soup and fish. Which component of the meal is the main source of carbohydrate?
questions.rationale: Banku is prepared mainly from fermented maize dough and provides substantial carbohydrate. Fish contributes protein and fat, while okro provides fibre, vitamins and minerals.

questions.question_text: A patient recovering from surgery requires additional dietary protein to support wound healing. Which Ghanaian food combination would provide a useful source of protein?
questions.rationale: Beans and fish provide dietary protein containing amino acids required for tissue repair and wound healing. The patient's overall intake should also provide sufficient energy and micronutrients.

questions.question_text: A nurse advises a patient to increase dietary fibre to help prevent constipation. Which food choice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Whole grains, beans, fruits and vegetables

questions.rationale: Dietary fibre increases stool bulk and can improve bowel movement regularity. Whole grains, legumes, fruits and vegetables are useful sources of fibre, and adequate fluid intake is also important.

questions.question_text: A patient frequently consumes large portions of fried foods and fatty meat. Which health risk may increase if this eating pattern contributes to excessive energy intake over time?

choices.text: Vitamin C deficiency in every case
Improved insulin sensitivity in every case

questions.rationale: Fats are energy-dense, providing approximately 9 kilocalories per gram. Regular consumption of excessive energy, including from fried foods, can contribute to weight gain and obesity.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman is advised to consume iron-rich foods. Which food combination may improve the absorption of non-haem iron?

choices.text: Beans eaten with orange or another vitamin C-rich fruit

questions.rationale: Vitamin C enhances the absorption of non-haem iron found in plant foods such as beans. Tea and coffee contain polyphenols that can reduce non-haem iron absorption when consumed with meals.

questions.question_text: A child develops swollen gums and poor wound healing after a prolonged diet lacking fresh fruits and vegetables. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.rationale: Vitamin C is required for collagen synthesis and normal connective tissue formation. Deficiency can cause scurvy, characterised by bleeding gums, poor wound healing and easy bruising.

questions.question_text: A schoolchild has an enlarged thyroid gland and lives in an area where dietary iodine intake is low. Which deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.rationale: Iodine is required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones. Inadequate iodine intake can cause thyroid enlargement (goitre) and impair growth and neurodevelopment.

questions.question_text: A woman weighs 72 kg and is 1.60 metres tall. What is her approximate body mass index?
questions.rationale: BMI is calculated as weight divided by height squared: 72 ÷ (1.60 × 1.60) = 28.1 kg/m². This falls within the adult overweight range of 25.0–29.9 kg/m².

questions.question_text: A nurse is assessing the nutritional status of a child under five years at a CHPS compound. Which measurement is particularly useful for identifying acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months?
questions.rationale: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a practical screening measurement for acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months. A MUAC below 115 mm indicates severe acute malnutrition, while 115 mm to less than 125 mm indicates moderate acute malnutrition under standard WHO classification.

questions.question_text: During nutritional assessment, a nurse asks a patient to describe all foods and drinks consumed during the previous 24 hours. Which assessment method is being used?
questions.rationale: A 24-hour dietary recall involves asking an individual to report all foods and drinks consumed during the preceding day. It helps assess dietary intake, although one day's recall may not represent usual eating patterns.

questions.question_text: A child presents with bilateral pitting oedema, sparse discoloured hair and skin lesions. Which nutritional condition is most likely?
questions.rationale: Bilateral pitting oedema is a key clinical feature of kwashiorkor and other forms of nutritional oedematous malnutrition. Hair and skin changes may also occur and require comprehensive nutritional and medical assessment.

questions.question_text: A severely wasted child has visible ribs, marked loss of muscle and no bilateral pitting oedema. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
questions.rationale: Marasmus is characterised by severe wasting due to a prolonged deficit of energy and nutrients. The child typically has marked loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle without the defining bilateral pitting oedema of kwashiorkor.

questions.question_text: A patient with type 2 diabetes asks which meal is a more appropriate choice for blood glucose management. Which option should the nurse recommend?

choices.text: A large portion of white rice with a sweetened soft drink
A controlled portion of whole-grain food with vegetables and lean protein
A meal consisting entirely of refined sugar
Skipping all meals throughout the day

questions.rationale: A controlled portion of whole-grain carbohydrate combined with vegetables and lean protein can support more appropriate post-meal glucose control. Regular meal patterns and individualised carbohydrate planning are important for diabetes management.

questions.question_text: A patient with hypertension frequently eats salted fish, salted meat and heavily salted soups. What advice should the nurse provide?

choices.text: Increase the amount of salt added during cooking
Reduce salt and high-sodium foods and use herbs or spices for flavour

questions.rationale: Reducing sodium intake helps manage blood pressure in many individuals. Limiting heavily salted foods and using herbs, spices and other low-sodium flavourings can support adherence to a healthier diet.

questions.question_text: A patient with chronic kidney disease is advised to follow an individualised renal diet. Which dietary factor may require restriction depending on kidney function and laboratory results?
questions.rationale: Reduced kidney function can impair potassium excretion, resulting in hyperkalaemia. Potassium intake should be individualised according to renal function, serum potassium levels and the patient's treatment plan rather than restricted routinely in every patient.

questions.question_text: A patient with liver cirrhosis and ascites is advised to modify dietary intake. Which dietary adjustment is commonly recommended to help manage fluid accumulation?

choices.text: Restrict dietary sodium according to the treatment plan
Consume large amounts of salted foods

questions.rationale: Sodium restriction is commonly recommended in the management of cirrhosis with ascites because sodium retention contributes to fluid accumulation. Nutritional management should be individualised, and protein should not be routinely eliminated because malnutrition is common in cirrhosis.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman attending antenatal care asks why she has been prescribed iron and folic acid supplementation. Which explanation is most appropriate?

choices.text: They prevent all infections during pregnancy
They help prevent maternal anaemia and support normal fetal development
They replace the need for a balanced diet

questions.rationale: Iron supports haemoglobin production and helps meet increased maternal iron requirements, while folic acid supports DNA synthesis and fetal neural tube development. Supplementation should be taken according to antenatal care and national recommendations.

questions.question_text: A breastfeeding mother asks whether she should stop eating fish because she is producing breast milk. What is the most appropriate advice?

choices.text: Eat a varied balanced diet and choose fish varieties with low mercury levels
Eat only starchy foods until breastfeeding stops

questions.rationale: Fish provides protein and important nutrients, including omega-3 fatty acids, which can support maternal and infant health. Breastfeeding mothers should choose safe, low-mercury fish and follow food safety advice.

questions.question_text: A mother gives her two-month-old infant water in addition to breast milk because she believes the hot Ghanaian weather makes the baby thirsty. What should the nurse advise?

choices.text: Give water after every breastfeeding session
Continue exclusive breastfeeding because breast milk provides the infant's fluid requirements during the first six months
Replace breast milk with fruit juice

questions.rationale: Breast milk provides sufficient water for healthy infants during the first six months, even in hot climates. Giving additional water can increase the risk of contamination and reduce breast milk intake.

questions.question_text: A mother has a healthy six-month-old infant and asks when complementary feeding should begin. Which advice is correct?

choices.text: Introduce safe, nutritious complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding
Give only fruit juice until the child is one year old
Continue exclusive breastfeeding without complementary foods until twelve months

questions.rationale: Complementary feeding should begin at six months because breast milk alone no longer meets all the infant's nutritional requirements. Breastfeeding should continue alongside adequate, safe and age-appropriate complementary foods.

questions.question_text: A mother complains that her newborn frequently cries and believes that her breast milk is insufficient. Which practice would best support effective breastfeeding?

choices.text: Limit breastfeeding to once every six hours
Encourage responsive feeding and assess the infant's attachment and positioning
Give sugar water after every feed

questions.rationale: Responsive feeding and effective attachment support milk transfer and stimulate milk production. The nurse should assess feeding technique, infant output and weight gain before concluding that breast milk is insufficient.

questions.question_text: A food vendor prepares waakye in the morning and intends to sell the remaining food throughout the day. Which practice best reduces the risk of foodborne illness?

choices.text: Keep cooked food at unsafe room temperature throughout the day
Maintain hot food at a safe hot-holding temperature or refrigerate it promptly
Mix fresh food with old leftovers without reheating
Leave food uncovered to cool in a dusty environment

questions.rationale: Cooked foods should not remain for prolonged periods at temperatures that permit rapid bacterial growth. Safe hot holding or prompt cooling and refrigeration helps reduce the risk of foodborne illness.

questions.question_text: A patient develops vomiting and diarrhoea after eating food that was prepared under unhygienic conditions. Which explanation best describes the likely route of infection?
questions.rationale: Poor food hygiene can allow pathogenic microorganisms to contaminate food, which may then be ingested. Safe preparation, handwashing, adequate cooking and proper storage reduce this risk.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse identifies children with poor dietary diversity in a rural community. Which intervention would best improve their nutritional intake using locally available foods?

choices.text: Encourage families to depend on one staple food only
Educate caregivers to combine staples with legumes, animal-source foods and fruits or vegetables
Advise families to avoid all locally grown vegetables
Recommend replacing meals with sweetened drinks

questions.rationale: Dietary diversity improves the likelihood that children receive a broad range of essential nutrients. Combining staples such as maize, cassava or rice with beans, fish, eggs, fruits and vegetables can improve nutritional quality.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman from a low-income household reports that she frequently skips meals because she cannot afford a variety of foods. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Advise her to stop attending antenatal care
Provide practical nutrition education using affordable local foods and link her to available community support
Recommend expensive imported foods as the only solution
Tell her that nutrition has no effect on pregnancy outcomes

questions.rationale: Nutrition counselling should consider household income, food availability and cultural preferences. Affordable foods such as beans, eggs, groundnuts, seasonal vegetables and locally available fruits can improve dietary quality.

questions.question_text: A child under five years is identified with moderate acute malnutrition during community screening. What should the community health nurse do?

choices.text: Ignore the finding if the child has no fever
Assess the child, provide appropriate nutritional counselling and arrange follow-up or referral according to the protocol
Recommend that the child stop eating for one day
Discharge the child without documenting the measurement

questions.rationale: Moderate acute malnutrition requires assessment, nutritional support, counselling and monitoring. The nurse should follow the applicable community-based management and referral procedures, especially if medical complications are present.

questions.question_text: A nurse assesses an adult patient with a BMI of 16.5 kg/m². How should this result be classified?
questions.rationale: An adult BMI below 18.5 kg/m² is classified as underweight. A BMI of 16.5 kg/m² indicates moderate thinness and should prompt further nutritional assessment.

questions.question_text: A child has bowed legs, delayed growth and bone deformities. The caregiver reports limited exposure to vitamin D-rich foods. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Rickets is a disorder of bone mineralisation in growing children, commonly associated with vitamin D deficiency and inadequate calcium or phosphate availability. It can cause bone pain, growth impairment and deformities such as bowed legs.

questions.question_text: A patient with a long history of poor dietary intake develops numbness in the hands and feet, weakness and megaloblastic anaemia. Which deficiency should be considered?
questions.rationale: Vitamin B12 is required for normal red blood cell formation and neurological function. Deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia and neurological manifestations such as peripheral neuropathy.

questions.question_text: A patient with diabetes becomes pale, sweaty, confused and tremulous after taking insulin but missing a meal. What is the most likely nutritional and metabolic problem?
questions.rationale: Insulin lowers blood glucose, and missing a meal after insulin administration can cause hypoglycaemia. The patient requires immediate blood glucose assessment and prompt treatment according to the facility's hypoglycaemia protocol.

questions.question_text: A severely malnourished child is admitted with bilateral pitting oedema, poor appetite and lethargy. Which action should the nurse prioritise?

choices.text: Immediately provide a large high-protein meal
Assess for medical complications and initiate stabilisation according to the severe acute malnutrition protocol
Restrict all fluids without clinical assessment

questions.rationale: Severe acute malnutrition with oedema and lethargy can be associated with hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, infection and electrolyte disturbances. Initial management requires careful assessment and stabilisation, including cautious therapeutic feeding according to the appropriate protocol.

questions.question_text: A child with severe acute malnutrition is started on nutritional rehabilitation. The child develops sudden breathlessness, weakness and an irregular heartbeat. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Refeeding syndrome can occur when nutrition is reintroduced too rapidly after prolonged starvation, causing electrolyte shifts, particularly hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia. These disturbances can cause cardiac, respiratory and neurological complications and require urgent assessment.

questions.question_text: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with muscle weakness and a serum potassium level of 6.7 mmol/L. Which dietary advice is most appropriate while urgent medical management is arranged?

choices.text: Encourage large servings of bananas, oranges and avocado
Avoid high-potassium foods and follow an individualised renal diet plan
Increase intake of potassium-containing salt substitutes
Recommend unrestricted intake of dried fruits

questions.rationale: A potassium concentration of 6.7 mmol/L indicates significant hyperkalaemia, which can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Dietary potassium restriction may be required, but urgent clinical assessment and treatment must not be delayed.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks' gestation presents with severe pallor, dizziness, breathlessness at rest and a very low haemoglobin concentration. What should the nurse prioritise?

choices.text: Advise her to take fruit juice and return after one month
Arrange urgent clinical assessment and management of severe anaemia
Reassure her that severe anaemia is a normal feature of pregnancy

questions.rationale: Severe anaemia during pregnancy can compromise maternal health and fetal oxygen delivery, particularly when accompanied by breathlessness and dizziness. Urgent assessment is required to determine the cause and appropriate treatment, including iron therapy or transfusion when clinically indicated.

questions.question_text: A six-month-old infant is fed thin maize porridge diluted with large quantities of water and receives no other complementary foods. The infant is failing to gain weight. What is the most appropriate nursing intervention?

choices.text: Advise the caregiver to continue the same feeding pattern until one year
Educate the caregiver on age-appropriate, nutrient-dense complementary foods, adequate feeding frequency and continued breastfeeding
Stop breastfeeding and provide water only
Recommend that the infant eat only adult solid foods

questions.rationale: Thin, heavily diluted porridge may provide insufficient energy and nutrients for an infant's needs. Complementary foods should be thick, nutrient-dense, safe and age-appropriate, with breastfeeding continued.

questions.question_text: Several people develop vomiting and diarrhoea after eating rice and stew that had been cooked the previous day and left at room temperature overnight. Which explanation is most likely?

choices.text: Food contamination and bacterial multiplication or toxin production during unsafe storage
The rice lost all its carbohydrates overnight
Refrigeration caused the food to become infectious
The food became contaminated because it contained protein

questions.rationale: Cooked rice left at room temperature can support the growth of Bacillus cereus, which may produce toxins associated with food poisoning. Prompt cooling, refrigeration and thorough reheating where appropriate reduce the risk, although some preformed toxins may resist reheating.

questions.question_text: A community nutrition survey identifies a high prevalence of anaemia among pregnant women. Which community-level intervention would most effectively address common nutritional causes while supporting maternal health?

choices.text: Discourage pregnant women from attending antenatal clinics
Strengthen antenatal nutrition education, iron-folic acid supplementation, screening and referral
Advise all women to avoid legumes and green leafy vegetables
Recommend tea with every meal to improve iron absorption

questions.rationale: Anaemia in pregnancy may result from iron deficiency, folate deficiency, infections and other causes. A combined approach involving screening, appropriate supplementation, dietary education and management of underlying conditions is more effective than dietary advice alone.

questions.question_text: A child aged 18 months is brought to a CHPS compound with poor weight gain, visible wasting and a MUAC measurement of 110 mm. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?

choices.text: The measurement is normal; routine follow-up is sufficient
The child has severe acute malnutrition and requires urgent assessment and management or referral
The child is overweight and should reduce food intake
The child has normal nutritional status because MUAC is only used in adults

questions.rationale: For children aged 6–59 months, a MUAC below 115 mm indicates severe acute malnutrition. The child requires prompt assessment for medical complications and management according to the relevant severe acute malnutrition protocol.

questions.question_text: A patient with hypertension and type 2 diabetes regularly consumes large portions of jollof rice, fried meat and sweetened drinks. Which dietary intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Recommend eliminating all food groups immediately
Develop an individualised meal plan with controlled portions, reduced sodium, limited added sugars and more vegetables
Encourage larger portions to prevent low blood pressure
Replace meals with sweetened fruit drinks

questions.rationale: The patient needs a sustainable dietary pattern that addresses both blood glucose and blood pressure. Portion control, reduced sodium, limited added sugars, appropriate carbohydrate choices and increased vegetable intake can support management of both conditions.

questions.question_text: A breastfeeding mother reports severe breast pain, fever and a swollen, red area on one breast. She wants to stop breastfeeding immediately. What is the most appropriate nursing advice?

choices.text: Stop breastfeeding permanently without clinical assessment
Arrange prompt assessment for mastitis and support continued breastfeeding or milk expression when appropriate
Restrict all fluid intake until the fever resolves
Apply unclean substances to the breast and avoid seeking care

questions.rationale: Fever, breast pain and localised redness may indicate mastitis, which requires prompt assessment and appropriate treatment. Continued breastfeeding or milk expression is generally encouraged when clinically appropriate because milk removal can support recovery.

questions.question_text: A caregiver refuses to give a child eggs and fish because of a cultural food taboo, despite the child having poor growth. What should the community health nurse do first?

choices.text: Criticise the caregiver's beliefs and end the consultation
Explore the caregiver's concerns respectfully and provide culturally appropriate nutrition education with acceptable alternatives
Force the caregiver to feed the child the restricted foods
Advise the caregiver to feed the child only maize porridge

questions.rationale: Food beliefs and taboos can influence dietary diversity and nutritional status. Respectful counselling should explore the reasons for avoidance and identify culturally acceptable alternatives that provide adequate protein and micronutrients.
